items.stem: Define the term 'product life cycle'.
items.answer: The stages a product goes through from its introduction, through growth and maturity, to decline.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The stages a product goes through from its introduction, through growth and maturity, to decline. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two extension strategies a business could use for a product in the maturity stage.
items.answer: It could find new markets, for example by exporting; or it could update the product's design or packaging so that it appeals to customers again.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark strategy, 1 mark explanation): new markets, new uses, redesign, new packaging, promotion. [4]

items.stem: Explain why a business should have a balanced product portfolio.
items.answer: Products at different stages spread risk; cash from mature products (cash cows) can fund new products, so the business is not dependent on one product.
items.markingKey: 1 mark spread risk; 1 mark cash from mature funds new; 1 mark avoid dependence. [3]

items.stem: Based in Karachi, Indus Sports Goods Ltd (private limited company) makes hand-stitched and machine-stitched footballs and cricket equipment. The business has around 950 employees. A rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices. Explain how Indus Sports could use the product life cycle to plan its marketing of footballs and cricket equipment.
items.answer: Points to develop for Indus Sports: the product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages; promotion and pricing change at each stage; extension strategies in maturity; timing the launch of smart footballs with built-in sensors.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: the product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Indus Sports (sports equipment manufacturing). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. promotion and pricing change at each stage; extension strategies in maturity. [3]

items.answer: Points to develop for Nile Pharma: the product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages; promotion and pricing change at each stage; extension strategies in maturity; timing the launch of over-the-counter vitamin supplements.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: the product life cycle has introduction, growth, maturity and decline stages. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Nile Pharma (pharmaceuticals). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. promotion and pricing change at each stage; extension strategies in maturity. [3]

items.stem: Han River Games is a private limited company in Seoul, South Korea with about 340 staff. It develops mobile games that earn revenue from in-game purchases. One game earns 70% of its revenue and its popularity is starting to fall. Evaluate whether Han River Games should use an extension strategy for its existing mobile games or launch a subscription gaming service.
items.answer: For: extension is cheaper and uses brand loyalty; new product gives long-term growth; portfolio balance. Against: extension may only delay decline; new products often fail; both need investment. Judgement: for Han River Games it depends mainly on the stage of the existing product, and also on the finance available.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts. AO4 Evaluation [3]: a justified judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the stage of the existing product; the finance available; market research evidence. A top-level answer reaches a supported conclusion specific to Han River Games. [10]

items.stem: At which stage of the product life cycle are sales highest?
items.answer: Maturity

items.stem: Define the term 'brand'.
items.answer: A name, symbol or design that identifies a product and distinguishes it from those of competitors.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – A name, symbol or design that identifies a product and distinguishes it from those of competitors. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two benefits to a business of having a strong brand.
items.answer: Customers are loyal and repeat their purchases, giving stable sales; and demand is less price elastic, so a premium price can be charged.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark benefit, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a USP is important in a competitive market.
items.answer: It gives customers a clear reason to choose this product over rivals, helping the business win sales and charge a higher price.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason to choose; 1 mark higher sales/price. [2]

items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: a brand identifies and differentiates products. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Hamid Engineering (engineering). AO3 Analysis [1]: developed explanation of the consequence, e.g. loyalty and repeat purchases; less price elastic demand. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'cost-plus pricing'.
items.answer: Setting the price by adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost of a product.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – Setting the price by adding a fixed percentage mark-up to the unit cost of a product. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of cost-plus pricing.
items.answer: Advantage: it is simple and ensures each unit covers its cost. Disadvantage: it ignores demand and competitors' prices, so the price may be too high to sell or too low to maximise profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage, 1 mark explanation; 1 mark disadvantage, 1 mark explanation. [4]

items.stem: Explain why a business might use price skimming for a new product.
items.answer: Early adopters are willing to pay a high price for something new, so the business earns high margins and can recover development costs quickly before competitors enter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark early adopters; 1 mark recover development costs/high margin. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'price elasticity of demand (PED)'.
items.answer: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition – The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. 1 mark: partial definition or a relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two factors that affect the price elasticity of demand for a product.
items.answer: The number of close substitutes: more substitutes make demand more elastic; and whether the product is a necessity: necessities have inelastic demand.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark factor, 1 mark explanation): substitutes, necessity/luxury, proportion of income, brand loyalty, time. [4]

items.stem: Explain why knowing PED is useful to a business when setting prices.
items.answer: It shows how sales and revenue will respond to a price change: if demand is inelastic, raising price increases revenue; if elastic, cutting price increases revenue.
items.markingKey: 1 mark predict sales response; 1 mark revenue effect explained. [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Deccan Auto: PED measures responsiveness of demand to price; inelastic demand: a price rise increases revenue; elastic demand: a price cut increases revenue; helps forecast sales and production.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: PED measures responsiveness of demand to price. AO2 Application [1]: point linked to Deccan Auto (automotive components). items.answer: PED is calculated from past data and assumes other factors are unchanged, but competitors' prices, incomes and tastes may change.
